**Nancy Patricia Pelosi** ([/pəˈloʊsi/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*pə-LOH-see*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); née **D'Alesandro**; born March 26, 1940) is an American politician who was the 52nd [speaker of the United States House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives "Speaker of the United States House of Representatives"), serving from 2007 to 2011 and again from 2019 to 2023. A member of the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"), she was the [first female elected speaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women_in_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives#Firsts "Women in the United States House of Representatives") and the [first woman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_female_speakers_of_legislatures_in_the_United_States#Congress "List of female speakers of legislatures in the United States") to lead a major political party in either chamber of [Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress"), heading the [House Democrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_Democratic_Caucus "House Democratic Caucus") from 2003 to 2023. Her 20 years as a House party leader are tied with [Joe Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_W._Martin_Jr. "Joseph W. Martin Jr.")'s as the second-longest after [Sam Rayburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Rayburn "Sam Rayburn").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-3) Pelosi is in her 20th term, having served in the House since 1987, representing [California's 11th congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California's_11th_congressional_district "California's 11th congressional district"), which includes most of [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"). She is the dean of [California's congressional delegation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California's_congressional_delegations "California's congressional delegations").

The daughter of Representative [Thomas D'Alesandro Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_D'Alesandro_Jr. "Thomas D'Alesandro Jr."), Pelosi was born and raised in [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore"). She graduated from [Trinity College, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Washington_University "Trinity Washington University"), in 1962 and married businessman [Paul Pelosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Pelosi "Paul Pelosi") the next year. They moved to [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") before settling down in San Francisco with their children. Focused on raising her family, Pelosi entered politics in the 1960s as a volunteer for the Democratic Party. After years of party work, rising to chair the [state party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Democratic_Party "California Democratic Party"), she was first elected to Congress in a [1987 special election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_California's_5th_congressional_district_special_election "1987 California's 5th congressional district special election"). Pelosi steadily rose through the ranks of the House Democratic Caucus to be elected [House minority whip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_leaders_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives "Party leaders of the United States House of Representatives") in 2001[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-4) and elevated to [House minority leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_leaders_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives "Party leaders of the United States House of Representatives") a year later.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-cnn_Loughlin-5)

In the [2006 midterm elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_midterm_elections "2006 midterm elections"), Pelosi led the Democrats to a majority in the House for the first time in 12 years and was subsequently elected Speaker. She was the first woman to hold the office.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-washingtonpost_branigin-6) Until [2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election"), Pelosi was the highest-ranking woman in the [presidential line of succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_line_of_succession "United States presidential line of succession") in U.S. history. During her first speakership, Pelosi was a major opponent of the [Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War") as well as the [Bush administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_George_W._Bush "Presidency of George W. Bush")'s [attempts to partially privatize Social Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Security_debate_in_the_United_States "Social Security debate in the United States"). She then helped pass the [Obama administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Barack_Obama "Presidency of Barack Obama")'s landmark bills, including the [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act"), the [Dodd–Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dodd–Frank_Wall_Street_Reform_and_Consumer_Protection_Act "Dodd–Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act"), the [Don't Ask, Don't Tell Repeal Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Ask,_Don't_Tell_Repeal_Act "Don't Ask, Don't Tell Repeal Act"), the [American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Recovery_and_Reinvestment_Act_of_2009 "American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009"), and the [2010 Tax Relief Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_Relief,_Unemployment_Insurance_Reauthorization,_and_Job_Creation_Act_of_2010 "Tax Relief, Unemployment Insurance Reauthorization, and Job Creation Act of 2010"). Pelosi lost the speakership after the [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") retook the majority in the [2010 midterm elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_midterm_elections "2010 midterm elections"), but retained her role as leader of the House Democrats.

In the [2018 midterms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_midterms "2018 midterms"), Democrats regained majority control of the House, and Pelosi [was again elected speaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives_election "2019 Speaker of the United States House of Representatives election"). This made her the first former speaker to reclaim the gavel since [Sam Rayburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Rayburn "Sam Rayburn") in 1955. During her second speakership, the House [impeached](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_impeachment_in_the_United_States "Federal impeachment in the United States") President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") twice, [first in December 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_impeachment_of_Donald_Trump "First impeachment of Donald Trump") and [again in January 2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_impeachment_of_Donald_Trump "Second impeachment of Donald Trump"); the [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate"), unable to reach the two-thirds majority necessary for conviction, acquitted Trump both times. She contributed to the passage of the [Biden administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biden_administration "Biden administration")'s principal bills, such as the [American Rescue Plan Act of 2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Rescue_Plan_Act_of_2021 "American Rescue Plan Act of 2021"), the [Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure_Investment_and_Jobs_Act "Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act"), the [CHIPS and Science Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CHIPS_and_Science_Act "CHIPS and Science Act"), and the [Inflation Reduction Act of 2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inflation_Reduction_Act_of_2022 "Inflation Reduction Act of 2022"). In the [2022 midterms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_midterm_elections "2022 midterm elections"), Republicans narrowly retook control of the House, ending her tenure as speaker. She subsequently retired as House Democratic leader, and was succeeded by [Hakeem Jeffries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hakeem_Jeffries "Hakeem Jeffries"). In November 2025, she announced she would not seek reelection in [2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections_in_California#District_11 "2026 United States House of Representatives elections in California") and would retire in January 2027.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-7) Considered an influential power broker in modern American politics, Pelosi has been regarded as a polarizing figure, drawing [criticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#Public_image) from both [conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism_in_the_United_States "Conservatism in the United States") and [progressives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressivism_in_the_United_States "Progressivism in the United States") for her [policy positions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#Political_positions), anti-populist rhetoric, and leadership style, and has faced scrutiny over issues such as the [Trump impeachments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Efforts_to_impeach_Donald_Trump "Efforts to impeach Donald Trump"), [insider trading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insider_trading "Insider trading") allegations, and moments seen by critics as emblematic of [liberal elitism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_elite "Liberal elite").

## Early life and education

Nancy Patricia D'Alesandro was born in [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore"), Maryland, to an [Italian-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian-American "Italian-American") family. She was the only daughter and the youngest of six children of Annunciata M. "Nancy" D'Alesandro (née Lombardi)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-baltimoremag-8) and [Thomas D'Alesandro Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_D'Alesandro_Jr. "Thomas D'Alesandro Jr.")[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-:2-9) Her mother, originating from [Fornelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fornelli "Fornelli") in [Southern Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Italy "Southern Italy"), emigrated to the U.S. in 1912;[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-10) her father traced his Italian ancestry to [Genoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa "Genoa"), [Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice "Venice") and [Abruzzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abruzzo "Abruzzo").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-:2-9)

At the time of Pelosi's birth, her father was a [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") congressman representing Maryland. He became mayor of Baltimore seven years later.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-:2-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-:D'AlesandroPoliticalFamily-11) Pelosi's mother was also active in politics, organizing Democratic women and teaching her daughter political skills.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-NYT010219-12) Her brother, [Thomas D'Alesandro III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_D'Alesandro_III "Thomas D'Alesandro III"), a Democrat, was elected Baltimore City Council president and later mayor, serving from 1967 to 1971.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-:D'AlesandroPoliticalFamily-11) As a child, Pelosi helped her father at his campaign events. Her affiliation with [liberalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberalism_in_the_United_States "Liberalism in the United States") sprouted in the 1960s; she was particularly impressed by President [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy")'s [inaugural address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inaugural_address_of_John_F._Kennedy "Inaugural address of John F. Kennedy").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-:2-9)

In 1958, Pelosi graduated from the [Institute of Notre Dame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Notre_Dame "Institute of Notre Dame"), an all-girls Catholic high school in Baltimore. She graduated from [Trinity College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Washington_University "Trinity Washington University") four years later with a [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") in [political science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science "Political science").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-13) Pelosi interned for Maryland senator [Daniel Brewster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Brewster "Daniel Brewster") in the 1960s alongside future House majority leader [Steny Hoyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steny_Hoyer "Steny Hoyer").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-14)

## Early career

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/President_John_F._Kennedy_Attends_Swearing-In_of_Thomas_D%27Alesandro.jpg/250px-President_John_F._Kennedy_Attends_Swearing-In_of_Thomas_D%27Alesandro.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_John_F._Kennedy_Attends_Swearing-In_of_Thomas_D'Alesandro.jpg)Pelosi, her mother, and President [John F. Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy "John F. Kennedy") watch as her father is sworn in as a member of the Renegotiation Board, 1961.

After moving to [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco"), Pelosi became friends with 5th district congressman [Phillip Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillip_Burton "Phillip Burton").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-15) In 1976, she was elected as a [Democratic National Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_National_Committee "Democratic National Committee") member from California, a position she would hold until 1996.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Guardian-16) She was elected party chair for Northern California in 1977 and four years later was selected to head the [California Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Democratic_Party "California Democratic Party"), which she led until 1983. Pelosi served as the San Francisco [Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Democratic_National_Convention "1984 Democratic National Convention") Host Committee chairwoman in 1984 and [Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Senatorial_Campaign_Committee "Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee") finance chair from 1985 to 1986.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-FastFacts-17)

## Early U.S. House of Representatives career

Phillip Burton died in 1983 and his wife, [Sala Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sala_Burton "Sala Burton"), won a [special election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/By_election "By election") to fill the remainder of her husband's congressional term and was reelected to two more terms. Burton decided not to run for reelection in 1988 and wanted Pelosi to succeed her, guaranteeing Pelosi the support of the Burtons' contacts.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-nationnewface-18) After Sala Burton's death, Pelosi won the [special election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_California's_5th_congressional_district_special_election "1987 California's 5th congressional district special election") to succeed her.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-19)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-20)

Pelosi has continued to represent approximately the same area of San Francisco for her entire congressional career, despite the boundaries shifting marginally in decennial post-[reapportionment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reapportionment "Reapportionment") [redistrictings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redistricting "Redistricting"). This area has been represented in the House by Democrats uninterruptedly since 1949, and is strongly Democratic-leaning (as of 2006, 13% of registered voters in the boundaries of Pelosi's district were Republican). It has not seen a serious Republican congressional contender since the early 1960s.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Edward1-21) Pelosi has been reelected to the House 18 times[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-22) without any substantive opposition. Unlike in her 1987 campaign, Pelosi has not participated in candidates' debates in her reelection campaigns. In her first seven reelection campaigns (from 1988 through 2004), she won an average of 80% of the vote.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Edward1-21)

When Pelosi took office, there were only 23 women in the House.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Calmes_LATimes-23) The AIDS epidemic was at a dire point.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Najjar1-24) San Francisco was greatly affected; its large population of gay men was the epidemic's initial epicenter.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-25) Beginning in her first term, Pelosi became a prominent congressional advocate on behalf of those impacted by HIV/AIDS.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Najjar1-24) Shortly after she took office, she hired a gay man as her congressional office's director of AIDS policy. In her first floor speech, Pelosi promised that she would be an advocate in the fight against what she called "the crisis of AIDS". With great stigma around the subject, some in her party privately chastised her for associating herself with it.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-FightForSF1-26) Pelosi co-authored the [Ryan White CARE Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_White_CARE_Act "Ryan White CARE Act"), which allocated funding dedicated to providing treatment and services for those impacted by HIV/AIDS.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Najjar1-24) President [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") signed the bill into law in December 1990.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-27)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Nancy_Pelosi_1993_congressional_photo.jpg/250px-Nancy_Pelosi_1993_congressional_photo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nancy_Pelosi_1993_congressional_photo.jpg)Pelosi as a member of the U.S. House of Representatives, 1993

Pelosi voted for the [Abandoned Shipwrecks Act of 1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abandoned_Shipwrecks_Act "Abandoned Shipwrecks Act").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-28) The Act asserts United States title to certain abandoned shipwrecks on or embedded in submerged lands under state jurisdiction, and transfers title to the respective state, thereby empowering states to manage these cultural and historical resources more efficiently, with the goal of preventing [treasure hunters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasure_hunting "Treasure hunting") and salvagers from damaging them. President [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") signed it into law on April 28, 1988.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-29)

In March 1988, Pelosi voted for the [Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Restoration_Act_of_1987 "Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1987") (and to override Reagan's veto).[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-32)

Pelosi helped shape the [Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brady_Handgun_Violence_Prevention_Act "Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act"), working with California Senator [Dianne Feinstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dianne_Feinstein "Dianne Feinstein") and New York Congressman [Chuck Schumer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Schumer "Chuck Schumer"). It became law in 1994.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-economist2023-33) Pelosi also held chairs on important [committees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_House_of_Representatives_committees "List of United States House of Representatives committees"), such as the [House Appropriations Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_Appropriations_Committee "House Appropriations Committee") and the [House Intelligence Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_Intelligence_Committee "House Intelligence Committee").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-economist2023-33)

In 2001, Pelosi was elected the House minority whip, second-in-command to Minority Leader [Dick Gephardt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Gephardt "Dick Gephardt"). She was the first woman in U.S. history to hold that post.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-34) Pelosi defeated [John Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lewis "John Lewis") and [Steny Hoyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steny_Hoyer "Steny Hoyer") for the position. A strong fundraiser, she used campaign contributions to help persuade other members of Congress to support her candidacy.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-LastBattle1-35)

Pelosi served on the [Appropriations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Committee_on_Appropriations "United States House Committee on Appropriations") and [Intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Permanent_Select_Committee_on_Intelligence "United States House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence") Committees and was the [ranking member](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranking_member "Ranking member") on the latter until her election as minority leader.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-36)

In 2002, Pelosi opposed the [Iraq Resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_Resolution "Iraq Resolution") authorizing President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") to use [military force against Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_invasion_of_Iraq "2003 invasion of Iraq"), which passed the House on a 296–133 vote.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-HouseClerk-37)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-MitchellIraq-38) She said, "unilateral use of force without first exhausting every diplomatic remedy and other remedies and making a case to the American people will be harmful to our war on terrorism."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-House2-39)

### Role as a Democratic Party fundraiser

Early in her political career, Pelosi established herself as a prominent fundraiser in the party.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-LastBattle1-35) She was one of the party's most prolific fundraisers, transferring significant funds to committees for other candidates.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Besnahan-41) During the 2000 and 2002 election cycles, among members of Congress, she contributed the most money to other congressional campaigns.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-42) In 2006, Pelosi was the Democratic Party's third-largest fundraiser, behind former first couple [Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") and [Hillary Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton "Hillary Clinton").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-ABCNov82006-43) From 2003 to 2014, Pelosi raised more than $400 million in campaign funds.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Besnahan-41)

## First tenure as minority leader (2003–2007)

In November 2002, after Gephardt resigned as House minority leader to seek the Democratic nomination in the [2004 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_presidential_election "2004 United States presidential election"), Pelosi was elected to replace him, becoming the first woman to lead a major party in either chamber of Congress.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-44) In the campaign to succeed Gephardt as the [House Democratic Caucus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_Democratic_Caucus "House Democratic Caucus")'s leader, Pelosi was challenged by [Harold Ford Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Ford_Jr. "Harold Ford Jr.") and [Marcy Kaptur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcy_Kaptur "Marcy Kaptur"). Kaptur withdrew her candidacy for the position before the November 15, 2002, caucus vote, and Pelosi defeated Ford 117–29 in the closed-door vote of caucus members.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-cnn_Loughlin-5) Critics of Pelosi characterized her as too liberal to be a successful House leader.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-45)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-46)

As minority leader, Pelosi sharply criticized the handling of the Iraq War by President Bush and his administration, in 2004 saying Bush had demonstrated areas of "incompetence".[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-47)

In a relative surprise, the Democratic Party lost three seats in the [2004 House elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections "2004 United States House of Representatives elections"), which coincided with [Bush's reelection as president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_presidential_election "2004 United States presidential election").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Billings2005a-48) Focused on retaking the House majority in 2006, in her second term as minority leader Pelosi worked to criticize the Bush administration more effectively and to contrast the Democratic Party with it.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Billings2005a-48)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-SandalowDetermination-49) As part of this, Pelosi voiced even harsher criticism of Bush's handling of the Iraq War.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-SandalowDetermination-49) In November 2005, prominent congressional Democrat [John Murtha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Murtha "John Murtha") proposed that the U.S. begin a withdrawal of troops from Iraq at the "earliest predictable date". Pelosi initially declined to commit to supporting Murtha's proposal.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-cbsnews_2005-50) Speaker [Dennis Hastert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Hastert "Dennis Hastert") soon brought to the floor a vote on a non-binding resolution calling for an immediate withdrawal of troops, seeking to trap Democrats into taking a more radical stance. Pelosi led Democrats in voting against the resolution, which failed in a 403–3 floor vote.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-cbsnews_2005-50) Roughly two weeks later, Pelosi held a press conference in which she endorsed Murtha's proposal.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-51) Some critics believed that Pelosi's support for a troop withdrawal would prevent the Democrats from winning a House majority in the [2006 elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections "2006 United States House of Representatives elections").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-SandalowDetermination-49)

During her time as minority leader, Pelosi was not well known to much of the American public. Before the 2006 elections, Republicans made a concerted effort to taint public perception of her, running advertisements assailing her.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-ABCNov82006-43) Advertisements demonizing Pelosi became a routine part of Republican advertising in subsequent elections.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Nolan1-52) For instance, during the 2022 election cycle, Republicans ran more than $50 million in ads that negatively characterized or invoked Pelosi, and in the 2010 cycle, they spent more than $65 million on such ads.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Nolan1-52)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Polman1-53)

## First speakership (2007–2011)

### 2007 speakership election

See also: [2007 Speaker of the United States House of Representatives election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives_election "2007 Speaker of the United States House of Representatives election")

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/Bush%2C_Pelosi%2C_and_Hoyer_meeting_at_White_House%2C_Nov_9%2C_2006.jpg/250px-Bush%2C_Pelosi%2C_and_Hoyer_meeting_at_White_House%2C_Nov_9%2C_2006.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bush,_Pelosi,_and_Hoyer_meeting_at_White_House,_Nov_9,_2006.jpg)President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") meets with [Speaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_(politics) "Speaker (politics)")-designate Pelosi and House Minority Whip [Steny Hoyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steny_Hoyer "Steny Hoyer") on November 9, 2006.

In the 2006 elections, the Democrats took control of the House, picking up 30 seats,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-54) the party's largest House seat gain since the [1974 elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections "1974 United States House of Representatives elections") held in the wake of the [Watergate scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watergate_scandal "Watergate scandal").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-SandalowDetermination-49) The party's House majority meant that as the party's incumbent House leader, Pelosi was widely expected to become speaker in the next Congress.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-ABCNov82006-43)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-55) On November 16, 2006, the Democratic caucus unanimously nominated her for speaker.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-56)

Pelosi supported her longtime friend John Murtha for House majority leader, the second-ranking post in the House. His competitor was House Minority Whip [Steny Hoyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steny_Hoyer "Steny Hoyer"), who had been Pelosi's second-in-command since 2003.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-57) Hoyer was elected House majority leader over Murtha by a margin of 149–86.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-CNN-58)

On January 4, 2007, Pelosi defeated Republican [John Boehner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Boehner "John Boehner") of Ohio, 233 votes to 202, in the election for speaker of the House.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-59)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-61)

[Rahm Emanuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rahm_Emanuel "Rahm Emanuel"), the incoming chairman of the House Democratic Caucus, nominated Pelosi, and her longtime friend [John Dingell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Dingell "John Dingell") swore her in, as the [dean of the House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dean_of_the_House_of_Representatives "Dean of the House of Representatives") traditionally does.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-62)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-washingtonpost_branigin-6)

[https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/5/56/2007_State_of_the_Union_Address_%E2%80%93_George_W._Bush_Library.webm/2007_State_of_the_Union_Address_%E2%80%93_George_W._Bush_Library.webm.240p.vp9.webm#t=16](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/5/56/2007_State_of_the_Union_Address_%E2%80%93_George_W._Bush_Library.webm/2007_State_of_the_Union_Address_%E2%80%93_George_W._Bush_Library.webm.240p.vp9.webm#t=16)

Pelosi (right) with Vice President [Dick Cheney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Cheney "Dick Cheney") behind President George W. Bush at the [2007 State of the Union Address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_State_of_the_Union_Address "2007 State of the Union Address"). Pelosi became the first woman to sit behind the podium at such an address. Bush acknowledged this by beginning his speech with the words, "Tonight, I have the high privilege and distinct honor of my own as the first president to begin the State of the Union message with these words: *Madam Speaker*."[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-63)

Pelosi was the first woman, the first Californian, and the first Italian-American to hold the speakership. She was also the second speaker from a state west of the [Rocky Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rocky_Mountains "Rocky Mountains"). The first was [Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_(state) "Washington (state)")'s [Tom Foley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Foley "Tom Foley"), the last Democrat to hold the post before Pelosi.

During her speech, she discussed the historical importance of being the first woman to hold the position of Speaker:
> This is a historic moment—for the Congress, and for the women of this country. It is a moment for which we have waited more than 200 years. Never losing faith, we waited through the many years of struggle to achieve our rights. But women weren't just waiting; women were working. Never losing faith, we worked to redeem the promise of America, that all men and women are created equal. For our daughters and granddaughters, today, we have broken the [marble ceiling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_ceiling "Glass ceiling"). For our daughters and our granddaughters, the sky is the limit, anything is possible for them.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-110speech-64)

She also said Iraq was the major issue facing the [110th Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/110th_United_States_Congress "110th United States Congress") while incorporating some Democratic Party beliefs:
> The election of 2006 was a call to change—not merely to change the control of Congress, but for a new direction for our country. Nowhere were the American people more clear about the need for a new direction than in Iraq. The American people rejected an open-ended obligation to a war without end.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-110speech-64)

As speaker, Pelosi remained the leader of the House Democrats, as the speaker is considered the leader of the majority caucus. But by tradition, she did not normally participate in debate and almost never voted on the floor, though she had the right to do so as a member of the House. She was also not a member of any House committees, also in keeping with tradition.

Pelosi was reelected speaker in 2009.

### Public perception

During and after her first tenure as speaker, Pelosi was widely characterized as a polarizing political figure. Republican candidates often associated their Democratic opponents with her.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-65)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-66) Pelosi became the focus of heavy disdain by "mainstream" Republicans and [Tea Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea_Party_Movement "Tea Party Movement") Republicans alike,[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Chaddock-67) as well as from the left.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-:3-68)

As they had in 2006, Republicans continued to run advertisements that demonized Pelosi.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-69) Before the 2010 House elections, the [Republican National Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_National_Committee "Republican National Committee") prominently used a "Fire Pelosi" slogan in its efforts to recapture the House majority.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-70)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-cbs_codon-71) This slogan was rolled out hours after the House passed the [Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patient_Protection_and_Affordable_Care_Act "Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-cbs_codon-71) Republicans spent $65 million ahead of the 2010 elections on anti-Pelosi advertisements.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Polman1-53) Pelosi long remained a target of Republican attacks.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-WASHPOST1-72) Ads demonizing her have been credited with fostering intense right-wing ire toward her,[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-73) and have been seen as one of the top factors in her unpopularity with the public.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-LastBattle1-35)

### Social Security

Shortly after being reelected in 2004, President Bush claimed a [mandate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandate_(politics) "Mandate (politics)") for an ambitious second-term agenda and proposed reforming [Social Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_Security_(United_States) "Social Security (United States)") by allowing workers to redirect a portion of their Social Security withholding into stock and bond investments.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-74) Pelosi strongly opposed the plan, saying there was no crisis, and as minority leader she imposed intense party discipline on her caucus, leading them to near-unanimous opposition to the proposal, which was defeated.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-75)

### Blocking of impeachment proceedings against President Bush

In the wake of Bush's 2004 reelection, several leading House Democrats believed they should pursue [impeachment proceedings against him](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_to_impeach_George_W._Bush "Movement to impeach George W. Bush"), asserting that he had misled Congress about [weapons of mass destruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weapon_of_mass_destruction "Weapon of mass destruction") in [Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction "Iraq and weapons of mass destruction") and violated Americans' civil liberties by [authorizing warrantless wiretaps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NSA_warrantless_surveillance_controversy "NSA warrantless surveillance controversy").

In May 2006, with an eye on the upcoming midterm elections—which offered the possibility of Democrats taking back control of the House for the first time since 1994—Pelosi told colleagues that, while the Democrats would conduct vigorous oversight of Bush administration policy, an impeachment investigation was "off the table". A week earlier, she had told *[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post "The Washington Post")* that although Democrats would not set out to impeach Bush, "you never know where" investigations might lead.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-76)

After becoming speaker in 2007, Pelosi held firm against impeachment, notwithstanding strong support for it among her constituents. In the 2008 election, she withstood a challenge for her seat by antiwar activist [Cindy Sheehan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cindy_Sheehan "Cindy Sheehan"), who ran as an independent primarily because of Pelosi's refusal to pursue impeachment.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-77)

### The "Hundred Hours"

Main article: [100-Hour Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/100-Hour_Plan "100-Hour Plan")

Before the midterm elections, Pelosi announced that if Democrats gained a House majority, they would push through most of their agenda during the first 100 hours of the 110th Congress.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-78)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-79)

The "first hundred hours" was a play on President [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt")'s promise for quick action to combat the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") during his ["first hundred days"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Days_Congress "Hundred Days Congress") in office. Newt Gingrich, who became speaker of the House in 1995, had a similar 100-day agenda to implement his [Contract with America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contract_with_America "Contract with America").

### Opposition to Iraq War troop surge of 2007

Main article: [Iraq War troop surge of 2007](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War_troop_surge_of_2007 "Iraq War troop surge of 2007")

On January 5, 2007, reacting to suggestions from Bush's confidants that he would increase troop levels in Iraq (which he announced in a speech a few days later), Pelosi and Senate Majority Leader [Harry Reid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Reid "Harry Reid") condemned the plan. They sent Bush a letter reading:
> [T]here is no purely military solution in Iraq. There is only a political solution. Adding more combat troops will only endanger more Americans and stretch our military to the breaking point for no strategic gain. ... Rather than deploy additional forces to Iraq, we believe the way forward is to begin the phased redeployment of our forces in the next four to six months while shifting the principal mission of our forces there from combat to training, logistics, force protection, and counter-terror.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-80)

### 2008 Democratic National Convention

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/77/Barack_Obama_and_Nancy_Pelosi_at_DNC_%281%29.jpg/250px-Barack_Obama_and_Nancy_Pelosi_at_DNC_%281%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Barack_Obama_and_Nancy_Pelosi_at_DNC_(1).jpg)Pelosi and [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") shaking hands at the [2008 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Democratic_National_Convention "2008 Democratic National Convention")

Pelosi was named Permanent Chair of the [2008 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Democratic_National_Convention "2008 Democratic National Convention") in [Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver "Denver"), Colorado.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-81)

### Healthcare reform

Pelosi has been credited for spearheading Obama's health care law, the [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act"),[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-82) when it seemed doomed to defeat. After Republican [Scott Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Brown_(politician) "Scott Brown (politician)") won Democrat [Ted Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Kennedy "Ted Kennedy")'s former Senate seat in the [January 2010 Massachusetts special election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_special_election_in_Massachusetts,_2010 "United States Senate special election in Massachusetts, 2010"), costing Democrats their 60-seat [filibuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_filibuster "Senate filibuster")-proof majority, Obama agreed with his then chief of staff [Rahm Emanuel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rahm_Emanuel "Rahm Emanuel")'s idea to do smaller initiatives that could pass easily. But Pelosi dismissed Obama's compunction, mocking his scaled-back ideas as "kiddie care".[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-83) After convincing him that this was their only shot at health care reform because of the large Democratic majorities in Congress, she rallied her caucus as she began an "unbelievable marathon" of a two-month session to craft the bill, which passed the House 219–212. In Obama's remarks before signing the bill into law, he called Pelosi "one of the best speakers the House of Representatives has ever had."[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-84)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-healthcarereform-85)[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-86)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-nytimesmagazinehealthcare-87)

### Assessments of first speakership

By early 2010, analysts were assessing Pelosi as possibly the most powerful woman in U.S. history and among the most powerful speakers of the previous 100 years.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Guardian-16) In March 2010, [Mark Shields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Shields "Mark Shields") wrote:
> In the last four months, [Pelosi] has not once, not twice but on three separate occasions done what none of her predecessors—including legendary giants [Tip O'Neill and Sam Rayburn]—could ever do: persuade the House of Representatives to pass national health-care reform. Pelosi has proved herself to be the most powerful woman in U.S. political history.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-88)

Later in 2010, Gail Russell Chaddock of *[The Christian Science Monitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Christian_Science_Monitor "The Christian Science Monitor")* opined that Pelosi was the "most powerful House speaker since Sam Rayburn a half century ago", adding that she had also been "one of the most partisan".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Chaddock-67) Scholars favorably assessed Pelosi's first speakership. In late 2010, [Norman Ornstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Ornstein "Norman Ornstein"), a congressional scholar at the conservative-leaning [American Enterprise Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Enterprise_Institute "American Enterprise Institute"), opined that despite polarized public opinion of Pelosi, "she's going to rank quite high in the pantheon of modern speakers", declaring that the only speaker of the previous 100 years he would rank higher than Pelosi was [Sam Rayburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Rayburn "Sam Rayburn"). [Catholic University of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_University_of_America "Catholic University of America") political scientist Matthew Green opined that the [111th Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/111th_Congress "111th Congress") had "been remarkable in its productivity—in both the number of bills enacted and their scope—and Pelosi shares much of the credit."[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-89) Green considered Pelosi's tenure as speaker to be among the greatest in U.S. history, highlighting the passage of the Affordable Care Act ("a measure with far-reaching implications for our nation's health care policy"). He also praised Pelosi for occasionally allowing House passage of measures that had majority overall House support but were opposed by the majority of the Democratic House Caucus. He noted that she had occasionally allowed bills to move forward in such fashion despite a high level of [political polarization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_polarization "Political polarization") in the United States.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-90)

In November 2010, Brian Naylor of [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR") opined that:
> During Nancy Pelosi's four years as speaker of the House, Congress approved the health care overhaul—widely considered the most significant piece of domestic legislation since Medicare—along with an $800 billion measure to stimulate the economy and a multi-billion-dollar rescue of the banks. It is a legislative legacy that rivals the accomplishments of any speaker in modern times.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-91)

In November 2010, after Democrats lost their House majority, *[Politico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politico "Politico")* writer John Bresnahan called Pelosi's record as speaker "mixed". He opined that Pelosi had been a powerful speaker, describing her as wielding "an iron fist in a Gucci glove" and having held "enormous power within the House Democratic Caucus", but noting that she had a "horrible approval rating with the rest of America". Bresnahan wrote that Pelosi's leadership and the legislative agenda she advanced had significantly contributed to the party's loss of its House majority, citing the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act as an example of legislation that hurt the Democrats electorally in 2010. Bresnahan also believed that, ahead of the 2010 elections, Pelosi had "disastrously" misread public opinion, and that Pelosi had been a poor orator.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-92)

Thomas Mann of the [Brookings Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookings_Institution "Brookings Institution") opined in 2018 that Pelosi had been the "strongest and most effective speaker of modern times" during her first speakership.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Beinart1-93)

In 2018, [Robert Draper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Draper "Robert Draper") wrote for *[The New York Times Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times_Magazine "The New York Times Magazine")*:
> During Nancy Pelosi's four years as speaker, there was no confusion as to who was in control. Pelosi used the tools at her disposal—committee assignments, campaign donations—to establish a balance among her party's coalitions while also reminding everyone that her job was not simply to officiate and appease...But as [Newt Gingrich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newt_Gingrich "Newt Gingrich") learned the hard way two decades ago, an autocratic speaker is a short-lived one. Pelosi's reign was successful because she understood the will of her caucus rather than bending it to hers.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-LastBattle1-35)

Draper also wrote that "for all her mastery of Washington's inside game, Pelosi has never been a deft public-facing politician," and called her a poor orator.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-LastBattle1-35)

## Second tenure as minority leader (2011–2019)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/80/Obama_meets_with_Congressional_Leadership_July_2011.jpg/250px-Obama_meets_with_Congressional_Leadership_July_2011.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Obama_meets_with_Congressional_Leadership_July_2011.jpg)President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") meets with congressional leadership, July 2011.

### 112th and 113th Congress

Though Pelosi was reelected by a comfortable margin in the [2010 elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections "2010 United States House of Representatives elections"), the Democrats lost 63 seats and control of the House of Representatives to the Republicans. After this setback, Pelosi sought to continue leading the House Democratic Caucus as minority leader, the office she held before becoming speaker. Intraparty opposition failed to pass a motion to delay the leadership vote,[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-94) though she faced a challenge from Representative [Heath Shuler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heath_Shuler "Heath Shuler"). Shuler lost to Pelosi, 150–43, in the caucus vote on November 17, 2010.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-95) On the opening day of the [112th Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/112th_United_States_Congress "112th United States Congress"), Pelosi was elected minority leader.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-96)

In November 2011, *[60 Minutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/60_Minutes "60 Minutes")* alleged that Pelosi and several other members of Congress had used information they gleaned from closed sessions to make money on the stock market. The program cited her purchases of [Visa Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visa_Inc. "Visa Inc.") stock while a bill that would limit credit card fees was in the House. Pelosi denied the allegations and called the report "a right-wing smear".[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-97)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-98)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-99) When the Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act (or [STOCK Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STOCK_Act "STOCK Act")) was introduced the next year, she voted for it and lauded its passing. Of representatives [Louise Slaughter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Slaughter "Louise Slaughter") and [Tim Walz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Walz "Tim Walz"), who drafted the bill, Pelosi said they "shined a light on a gaping hole in our ethics laws and helped close it once and for all".[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-100)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-101)

On November 14, 2012, Pelosi announced that she intended to remain Democratic leader.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-WaPoDL-102)

Pelosi was one of many lawmakers who called for the [Washington Redskins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Redskins "Washington Redskins") to change their name.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-103) She said it was time for the [U.S. Patent and Trademark Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Patent_and_Trademark_Office "United States Patent and Trademark Office") to step in and tell the [National Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League") that it could not keep its registered trademark for the "Redskins", a racial slur for [Native Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-104)

### 114th and 115th Congress

In August 2016, Pelosi said that her personal contact information had been posted online following a cyberattack against top Democratic campaign committees and she had received "obscene and sick calls, voice mails and text messages". She warned members of Congress to avoid letting children or family members answer phone calls or read text messages.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-105)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Nancy_Pelosi_%2816526886414%29.jpg/250px-Nancy_Pelosi_%2816526886414%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nancy_Pelosi_(16526886414).jpg)Pelosi speaking at the [United States Department of Labor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Labor "United States Department of Labor") on [Equal Pay Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_Pay_Day "Equal Pay Day")[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Pelosi_greets_DREAMers_fasting_outside_the_Capitol.jpg/250px-Pelosi_greets_DREAMers_fasting_outside_the_Capitol.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pelosi_greets_DREAMers_fasting_outside_the_Capitol.jpg)Pelosi greets [DREAMers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DREAMers "DREAMers") fasting outside the Capitol, September 2017.

At times, centrists, [progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left_liberal "Left liberal") candidates and incumbent Democrats all expressed opposition to Pelosi's continued tenure as the party's House leader.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-106)

Prompted by colleagues after the [2016 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election "2016 United States presidential election"), [Tim Ryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Ryan_(Ohio_politician) "Tim Ryan (Ohio politician)") of Ohio initiated a bid to replace Pelosi as House minority leader on November 17, 2016.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-107) After Pelosi agreed to give more leadership opportunities to junior members,[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-108) she defeated Ryan by a vote of 134–63 on November 30.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-109)

In 2017, after Democrats lost four consecutive special elections in the House of Representatives, Pelosi's leadership was again called into question. In June 2017, Representative [Kathleen Rice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathleen_Rice "Kathleen Rice") of New York and a small group of other House Democrats, including [Congressional Black Caucus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congressional_Black_Caucus "Congressional Black Caucus") chairman [Cedric Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedric_Richmond "Cedric Richmond"), held a closed-door meeting to discuss potential new Democratic leadership.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-110) Other House Democrats, including Ryan, [Seth Moulton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seth_Moulton "Seth Moulton"), and [Filemon Vela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filemon_Vela_Jr. "Filemon Vela Jr."), publicly called for new House leadership.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-:0-111) In an interview, Rice said, "If you were talking about a company that was posting losing numbers, if you were talking about any sports team that was losing time and time again, changes would be made, right? The CEO out. The coach would be out and there would be a new strategy put in place."[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-:0-111) In a press conference, Pelosi defended her leadership, saying, "I respect any opinion that my members have but my decision about how long I stay is not up to them."[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-:0-111) When asked specifically why she should stay on as House minority leader after numerous Democratic seats were lost, she responded, "Well, I'm a master legislator. I am a strategic, politically astute leader. My leadership is recognized by many around the country, and that is why I'm able to attract the support that I do."[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-112)

In November 2017, after Pelosi called for [John Conyers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Conyers "John Conyers")'s resignation over allegations of harassment, she convened the first in a series of planned meetings on strategies to address reforming workplace policies in the wake of national attention to sexual harassment. She said Congress had "a moral duty to the brave women and men coming forward to seize this moment and demonstrate real, effective leadership to foster a climate of respect and dignity in the workplace".[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-113)

In February 2018, Pelosi sent a letter to Speaker [Paul Ryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Ryan "Paul Ryan") about the proposed public release of a memo prepared by Republican staff at the direction of House Intelligence Committee Chairman [Devin Nunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Devin_Nunes "Devin Nunes"). The memo attacked the [Federal Bureau of Investigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") for its investigation of [Russian interference in the 2016 United States elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_interference_in_the_2016_United_States_elections "Russian interference in the 2016 United States elections"). Pelosi said the FBI and the Department of Justice had warned Nunes and Ryan that the memo was inaccurate and that its release could threaten national security by disclosing federal surveillance methods. She added that Republicans were engaged in a "cover-up campaign" to protect Trump: "House Republicans' pattern of obstruction and cover-up to hide the truth about the Trump-Russia scandal represents a threat to our intelligence and our national security. The GOP has led a partisan effort to distort intelligence and discredit the U.S. law enforcement and intelligence communities."[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-114) She charged Nunes with "deliberately dishonest actions" and called for his immediate removal from his position.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-115)

In February 2018, Pelosi broke the record for longest House speech using the "[magic minute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_minute "Magic minute")" custom when she spent more than eight hours recounting stories from [DREAMers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DREAMers "DREAMers")—people brought to the United States as minors by undocumented immigrants—to object to a budget deal that would raise spending caps without addressing the future of [DACA recipients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deferred_Action_for_Childhood_Arrivals "Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals"), who were at risk of deportation by the Trump administration.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-116)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-117)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-118)

In May 2018, after the White House invited two Republicans and no Democrats to a Department of Justice briefing on an FBI informant who had made contact with the Trump campaign,[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-119) Pelosi and Schumer sent a letter to Deputy Attorney General [Rod Rosenstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_Rosenstein "Rod Rosenstein") and FBI director Wray calling for "a bipartisan Gang of Eight briefing that involves congressional leadership from both chambers".[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-120)

In August 2018, Pelosi called for [Duncan D. Hunter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_D._Hunter "Duncan D. Hunter")'s resignation after his indictment on charges of misusing at least $250,000 in campaign funds, saying the charges were "evidence of the rampant culture of corruption among Republicans in Washington today".[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-121)

In April 2018, [Peter Beinart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Beinart "Peter Beinart") wrote in *[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic "The Atlantic")* that Pelosi had been "the most effective congressional leader of modern times—and, not coincidentally, the most vilified."[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Beinart1-93)

## Second speakership (2019–2023)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/Nancy_Pelosi_Official_Painting.jpg/250px-Nancy_Pelosi_Official_Painting.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nancy_Pelosi_Official_Painting.jpg)Official painting, 2022 (composed in 2014)

In the [2018 elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections "2018 United States House of Representatives elections"), the Democrats recaptured a House majority, gaining 41 seats. This was the party's largest gain in the House since the 1974 post-Watergate elections.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-122)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-123) On November 28, House Democrats nominated Pelosi to once again serve as speaker.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-124) She was [reelected to the speakership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Speaker_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives_election "2019 Speaker of the United States House of Representatives election") at the start of the [116th Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/116th_United_States_Congress "116th United States Congress") on January 3, 2019. Pelosi "clinched the speakership after weeks of whittling down opposition from some fellow Democrats seeking a new generation of leadership. The deal to win over holdouts put an expiration date on her tenure: she promised not to stay more than four years in the job". 220 House Democrats voted for Pelosi as Speaker and 15 for someone else or no one.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-125)

On February 4, 2020, at the conclusion of Trump's [State of the Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_the_Union "State of the Union") address, Pelosi tore up her official copy of it.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Samuels-TheHill-126) Her stated reason for doing so was "because it was a courteous thing to do considering the alternatives. It was a such a dirty speech".[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-127) Trump and other Republicans criticized her for this.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-128)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-129)

In December 2021, Pelosi announced her candidacy for reelection to the House in [2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections "2022 United States House of Representatives elections").[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-130) In 2018, and again in 2020, she had agreed not to stay on as speaker beyond January 2023, but otherwise avoided questions about her future.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-131) In 2022, Pelosi was reelected, but the Democratic Party lost the House majority.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-132) Ten days later, she announced that she would not seek a Democratic leadership post in the next Congress.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-133)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-134)

### 2018–2019 government shutdown

Main article: [2018–2019 United States federal government shutdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018–2019_United_States_federal_government_shutdown "2018–2019 United States federal government shutdown")

[https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/e/ec/President_Trump_Meets_with_the_Senate_Minority_Leader_and_the_House_Speaker-Designate.webm/President_Trump_Meets_with_the_Senate_Minority_Leader_and_the_House_Speaker-Designate.webm.240p.vp9.webm#t=932](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/e/ec/President_Trump_Meets_with_the_Senate_Minority_Leader_and_the_House_Speaker-Designate.webm/President_Trump_Meets_with_the_Senate_Minority_Leader_and_the_House_Speaker-Designate.webm.240p.vp9.webm#t=932)

President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") meets with Pelosi and Senate Minority Leader [Chuck Schumer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Schumer "Chuck Schumer") on December 11, 2018, saying "I will be the one to shut it down."

At the start of the 116th Congress, Pelosi opposed Trump's attempts to use the [2018–2019 federal government shutdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018–2019_United_States_federal_government_shutdown "2018–2019 United States federal government shutdown") (which she called a "hostage-taking" of civil servants) as leverage to build a substantial wall on the U.S.-Mexico border.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-135) She declined to allow Trump to give the [State of the Union Address](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_State_of_the_Union_Address "2019 State of the Union Address") in the House chamber while the shutdown was ongoing.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-136)[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-137) After several polls showed Trump's popularity sharply falling due to the shutdown, on January 25, 2019, Trump signed a stopgap bill to reopen the government without any concessions regarding a border wall for three weeks to allow negotiations on an appropriations bill. But he reiterated his demand for border wall funding and said he would shut the government down again or declare a national emergency and use military funding to build the wall if Congress did not appropriate the funds by February 15.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-138)

On February 15, Trump declared a national emergency in order to bypass Congress, after being unsatisfied with a bipartisan bill that had passed the House and Senate the day before.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-139)

### Impeachments of President Trump

Main articles: [First impeachment of Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_impeachment_of_Donald_Trump "First impeachment of Donald Trump") and [Second impeachment of Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_impeachment_of_Donald_Trump "Second impeachment of Donald Trump")

On September 29, 2019, Pelosi announced the launch of [an impeachment inquiry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_impeachment_inquiry_against_Donald_Trump "First impeachment inquiry against Donald Trump") against Trump.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-140) On December 5, 2019, after the inquiry had taken place, Pelosi authorized the Judiciary Committee to begin drafting articles of impeachment.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-141) After hearings were held,[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-142) two articles of impeachment were announced on December 10.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-143) The House of Representatives approved both articles on December 18, thereby formally impeaching Trump.[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-144)

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Nancy_Pelosi_signs_the_article_of_the_second_impeachment_of_Donald_Trump_24.png/250px-Nancy_Pelosi_signs_the_article_of_the_second_impeachment_of_Donald_Trump_24.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nancy_Pelosi_signs_the_article_of_the_second_impeachment_of_Donald_Trump_24.png)Pelosi signs the article of impeachment for the second impeachment of Donald Trump on January 13, 2021.

During the [January 6 United States Capitol attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/January_6_United_States_Capitol_attack "January 6 United States Capitol attack"), Pelosi's laptop and [gavel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavel "Gavel") were [stolen from her office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riley_Williams#Role_in_Capitol_attack "Riley Williams"). They have not been recovered.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-145) The day after the attack, Pelosi demanded that Trump either resign or be removed from office through the clauses of section four the [Twenty-Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twenty-Fifth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "Twenty-Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution"), threatening impeachment if this did not happen.[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-146) On January 10, she told Vice President [Mike Pence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Pence "Mike Pence") that if he did not invoke the 25th amendment within 24 hours, she would proceed with legislation to impeach Trump.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-147) On January 13, the House voted to impeach Trump a second time.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-148)

### COVID-19 pandemic and response

Main article: [COVID-19 pandemic in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States")

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/P20210312AS-2551_%2851102888325%29.jpg/250px-P20210312AS-2551_%2851102888325%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:P20210312AS-2551_(51102888325).jpg)Pelosi delivers remarks on the [American Rescue Plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Rescue_Plan_Act_of_2021 "American Rescue Plan Act of 2021") in March 2021.

This was contrary to regulations enforced at that time preventing service indoors.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-150) Criticized for hypocrisy by Trump and the owners of the salon, Pelosi described the situation as "clearly a setup". Her stylist and other Democrats defended her.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-151)

### Infrastructure bill

Pelosi played a key role in the 2021 passage of the [Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure_Investment_and_Jobs_Act "Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act").

*The New York Times* credited the legislation's passage to Pelosi's decision to adopt a Congressional Black Caucus proposal to pair together the final vote on the bill with a good-faith vote on the rules governing debate on a subsequent social safety net bill. The Times noted that Pelosi did not make herself the public face of this, instead having Congressional Black Caucus Chairwoman [Joyce Beatty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joyce_Beatty "Joyce Beatty") persuade House Democratic Caucus members to accept the proposal. The *New York Times* wrote, "in effect, the speaker had harnessed one faction of her unruly Democrats to win over two others."[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Cillizzamosteffective-152) [Chris Cillizza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Cillizza "Chris Cillizza") of [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN") wrote:
> Consider the challenge Pelosi faced with this infrastructure bill—starting with the fact that she had only a three-seat majority, meaning that even a handful of renegade Democrats could scuttle the entire thing. Then add in the total lack of trust not only between House liberals and Senate moderates but also the decided lack of trust between House liberals and House moderates. And sprinkle in the fact that the entire bill had been at an impasse for months as both sides of the party wrangled for leverage on the broader $1.75 trillion social safety net legislation.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Pelosi#cite_note-Cillizzamosteffective-152)
